passage: I only looked up because a dog barked. My phone had said the shortest route was left, so I went left, then left again, down a lane with no lights and a fence with barbed wire. The little blue dot kept moving, and I kept following it. It was late and the road ended at a locked gate beside a building site. My heart sank. There was nobody. I turned around and walked quickly back to the main road, where a chai stall was open, and asked the man where the station was. He pointed the other way. I still use the map, but now I glance up every few steps. Shalini

qa.q: What made Shalini look up from the phone?
qa.a: A dog barked.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when the road ended at a locked gate?
qa.a: Shalini felt alarmed and alone, since the heart sank and there was nobody around.

qa.q: What did Shalini do after noticing the danger, and what would you add?
qa.a: Shalini turned back to the main road and asked a stall owner, and could add that checking the surroundings sooner would have avoided the dark lane.

qa.q: What might the chai stall owner have thought when Shalini asked the way?
qa.a: The stall owner probably saw a lost traveller who had trusted the phone too much, and simply pointed the right way.

grounding: Shows a young traveller following a map app onto an unlit lane and only then looking up at what is actually around.

passage: Dusk in an unfamiliar town, and Dhruv had his eyes on his phone. "It says forty metres, then right." I walked beside him, watching the road. The right turn was a narrow lane with no pavement and no lights, where trucks were reversing. I said, "Are you sure?" but he was still reading the screen. A horn blared behind us. I grabbed his sleeve and pulled him against the wall. He looked up, pale, for the first time in ten minutes. We stopped at a tea shop and asked the owner for the walking route. Dhruv laughed, but his voice was thin. I did not say I told you so. Neelam

qa.q: What was in the narrow lane where the phone told Dhruv to turn?
qa.a: The narrow lane had no pavement and no lights, and trucks were reversing there.

qa.q: What might Neelam be feeling as Neelam walks beside Dhruv and watches the road?
qa.a: Neelam is probably worried and alert, noticing the danger while Dhruv reads the screen, and then relieved after the horn.

qa.q: What did Neelam and Dhruv do after the horn that was wise?
qa.a: They stopped at a tea shop and asked the owner for the walking route, checking the app against a local person.

qa.q: How does Dhruv seem to feel after looking up, and what is unclear?
qa.a: Dhruv looks pale and laughs in a thin voice, which suggests shock, though Neelam can only guess what he feels inside.

grounding: Shows a young traveller trusting a navigation app blindly onto an unsafe road until a horn makes him look up, as seen by a companion.

passage: I'm Tejas, and last winter I learned not to worship my phone's map. My friend Sharmila and I were riding a scooter from Mysuru to a waterfall. The map said, "Turn left for a shorter route." I turned without thinking. The road became gravel, then mud, then a narrow track through fields. It was getting dark. There were no houses, and the phone signal dropped to one bar. Sharmila tapped my shoulder. "Tejas, look around. Does this look like a road to anywhere?" For the first time in an hour, I actually looked. Only then did I feel the fear. We turned back to the main road, asked at a tea stall, and got there by the highway.

qa.q: Where were Tejas and Sharmila riding to?
qa.a: To a waterfall.

qa.q: When did Tejas start to feel afraid?
qa.a: Only after Sharmila's question, when Tejas finally looked around and saw the dark, empty track.

qa.q: What should Tejas do on the next trip?
qa.a: Use the map as a helper but keep noticing the road, turning back when it looks wrong and asking locals.

qa.q: How did Sharmila see the situation before Tejas did?
qa.a: Sharmila noticed that the track led nowhere and felt uneasy, prompting Tejas to look up.

grounding: A young traveller recalls following a map app onto an unsafe track and only then looking up and turning back.

passage:
Trek leader's note, Saturday.
Two of our group, Sarika and Chandrika, both twenty, left the main trail today to follow a "shortcut" shown on Sarika's phone map. The route led them onto a steep slope with loose scree, which the app shows as a path. Sarika kept looking at the screen, saying, "It says two hundred metres." Chandrika called me when the slope got dangerous. I reached them in fifteen minutes and guided them back along the ridge. Sarika was shaken and embarrassed. At dinner I reminded the group: the app helps, but look at the ground in front of you. From tomorrow, everyone stays on the marked trail.

qa.q: How far did the phone say the shortcut was?
qa.a: "It says two hundred metres."

qa.q: How did Sarika feel after being guided back?
qa.a: Sarika was shaken and embarrassed after following the screen onto a dangerous slope.

qa.q: What lesson did the trek leader give, and why does it matter?
qa.a: The app helps, but you must look at the ground in front of you, because the map showed a path where there was only loose scree.

qa.q: What did Chandrika do that helped keep them safe?
qa.a: Chandrika noticed the slope getting dangerous and called the trek leader.

grounding: A trek leader's note shows a young traveller following a map app onto an unsafe slope until someone looks up and calls for help.

passage:
Dear Diary, Thursday.
Such a silly, scary evening. I was going to Yash's cousin's house for dinner in a part of Hyderabad I'd never been to. I walked with my phone in my hand, following the blue dot, not looking anywhere else. The app took me down a lane that got darker and emptier, past a closed factory. A dog started barking. Only then did I look up and realise there were no people at all. My stomach dropped.
I walked back to the main road, fast, and called Yash, who came to meet me at the petrol pump.
The app wasn't wrong exactly. I just stopped using my own eyes.
Zainab

qa.q: Where did Yash come to meet Zainab?
qa.a: At the petrol pump.

qa.q: How did Zainab feel when looking up in the empty lane?
qa.a: Zainab felt frightened, stomach dropping, on realising there were no people around.

qa.q: What did Zainab do right once the danger was noticed?
qa.a: Zainab went back to the busy main road and called Yash to meet at a public place.

qa.q: How might Yash feel getting the call?
qa.a: Yash was likely worried and quick to help, glad Zainab called instead of pushing on.

grounding: A diary shows a young traveller following a map app blindly into an empty, unsafe lane and only then looking up.

passage:

Nilesh: what?? the map said 12 min via the canal road
Eshaan: it sent me onto the service road. no lights. trucks passing like a metre away
Eshaan: I only looked up when one honked. I was literally staring at the blue dot
Nilesh: stop. are you off the road?
Eshaan: yes, next to a closed dhaba, under its light
Nilesh: ok stay there. I'm coming on the scooter. share live location
Eshaan: shared
Eshaan: I feel so dumb. I cycled right past the canal turn. I SAW it. the map said keep straight
Nilesh: the map doesn't know the canal road is the lit one. you do
Nilesh: 10 min. don't move
Eshaan: not moving 🙏

qa.q: Where did Eshaan stop to wait?
qa.a: Next to a closed dhaba, under its light.

qa.q: How does Eshaan feel after looking up?
qa.a: Eshaan is shaken by the trucks and embarrassed, feeling dumb for ignoring the turn that was right there.

qa.q: What could Eshaan do differently next time the map disagrees with what is actually there?
qa.a: Glance up at junctions and trust local knowledge, like the lit canal road, using the map as a helper rather than the boss.

qa.q: How does Nilesh react to the messages?
qa.a: Nilesh is worried and acts quickly, telling Eshaan to get off the road, share a live location and wait while Nilesh comes on the scooter.
